answer: Nullifier-linked hardware tokens. Each identity is bound to a token whose secret maps to one public vertex in a sparse registry. For every action, the token emits a context-bound nullifier; if a secret is duplicated, two agents produce the same nullifier in that context, exposing the clone. An attacker must buy and enroll a fresh token per identity, absorb hardware and onboarding costs, and still risk linkage when a token is copied. The registry can tolerate churn like a tide, but each clone needs independent hardware. Audit logs retain an ivory marker for any reused nullifier.
